# Wearable Haptic Pattern Display Device for the Visually Impaired

## Overview

This disclosure presents an innovative wearable haptic pattern display device engineered specifically to address the daily accessibility challenges faced by blind and visually impaired users. The device is designed with portability and ease of use as core principles, ensuring that users can seamlessly integrate it into their daily routines without cumbersome setup or handling requirements.

## Core Technology: Integrated Touch and Haptic Display

At the heart of the device lies a sophisticated touch screen that combines touch-sensitive and electro-sensitive panel technologies. This integration allows the device to generate readable text through dynamically produced haptic textures. By varying the combination and arrangement of these tactile patterns, the device can represent a wide range of characters, words, and symbols, enabling users to "read" text through touch rather than sight. This tactile text generation system serves as a modern alternative to traditional braille, offering greater flexibility and potentially faster content delivery.

## Ergonomic Design for Hands-Free Convenience

A distinguishing feature of this device is its thoughtful ergonomic design, which incorporates a ring-shaped wearing member affixed to the back of the main body. This structural element allows users to secure the device directly onto their index finger, leaving their thumb free to actively scan and interpret the haptic text displayed on the screen. This intuitive one-handed operation eliminates the need to hold a separate reading device, freeing the user's other hand for additional tasks such as holding a cane, handrail, or other objects—a critical advantage for maintaining balance and safety while navigating real-world environments.

## Enhanced Accessibility and Independence

The combination of compact portability and intuitive finger-worn design empowers blind users to access written content—including news articles, books, and text messages—at any time and in virtually any location. Whether commuting, waiting in a public space, or relaxing at home, users gain the freedom to engage with information on their own schedule, without depending on sighted assistance or being restricted to specific locations equipped with accessibility technology. This capability significantly enhances the user's sense of independence and improves overall quality of life by reducing barriers to information access.

## NFC-Enabled Navigation and Contextual Information

To further extend the device's utility beyond text reading, an integrated Near Field Communication (NFC) module enables the device to interact with NFC tags strategically placed in the physical environment. These tags may be positioned at critical navigational points such as road crossings, intersections, store entrances, or alongside existing braille signage. When the device comes into proximity with an NFC tag, it automatically receives and processes location-specific guide information, which is then relayed to the user through the haptic display.

This feature transforms the device into a comprehensive navigation aid, allowing blind users to receive real-time contextual information about their surroundings. By bridging the gap between physical infrastructure and digital accessibility technology, the NFC integration helps users navigate unfamiliar environments with greater confidence, safety, and autonomy—effectively extending the device's functionality from a reading tool to a holistic mobility and information assistant.

## Conclusion

By combining advanced haptic display technology, ergonomic wearable design, and NFC-based environmental awareness, this device represents a comprehensive solution for enhancing the daily lives of blind and visually impaired individuals. It addresses both the need for on-demand access to written content and the practical challenges of navigating physical spaces, ultimately promoting greater independence and inclusion in everyday activities.

# Wearable Haptic Pattern Display Device for the Visually Impaired

## Technical Field

The present disclosure relates to an assistive technology device designed to enhance the daily lives of blind and visually impaired individuals. More specifically, it relates to a wearable haptic pattern display device that converts digital text and location-based information into tactile patterns that can be read through touch, thereby providing an intuitive and portable means of accessing written information and navigational guidance.

## Background

Individuals with visual impairments have traditionally relied on braille as the primary method for reading printed text. However, conventional braille materials—whether in book form or as embossed signage—present significant limitations. Braille books are often bulky, expensive to produce, and available only for a limited selection of titles. Braille signage installed in public spaces requires physical contact with fixed installations, and users must actively search for and locate such signs, which can be inconvenient or even hazardous in unfamiliar environments.

Furthermore, existing electronic braille displays, while offering some advantages over static braille materials, tend to be large, heavy, and expensive, limiting their practicality for everyday portable use. There remains a substantial need for a compact, affordable, and easily wearable device that allows blind users to access text-based information—such as news articles, digital books, and personal messages—as well as real-time location-based guidance, without being tethered to bulky equipment or specialized infrastructure.

## Summary of the Disclosure

To address these challenges, the present disclosure provides a wearable haptic pattern display device that is compact, lightweight, and easy to wear during everyday activities. The device is designed to be worn on the hand and read using the thumb, allowing for discreet and convenient operation in a wide variety of settings, including while walking, commuting, or sitting in public spaces.

### Main Body and Display Components

The core of the device is a compact main body sized to comfortably fit on the back of the hand or finger area. The front surface of the main body integrates two key components: a touch panel and an electro-sensitive haptic panel.

The touch panel allows the user to interact with the device—for example, to scroll through text, adjust settings, or select different reading modes—through simple touch gestures. Positioned beneath or alongside the touch panel, the electro-sensitive panel is responsible for physically rendering text as raised or vibrating tactile patterns. This panel employs an array of actuable elements (such as micro-pins, piezoelectric elements, or electroactive polymers) that can be dynamically raised, lowered, or vibrated to form braille characters or other tactile textures corresponding to the digital text being displayed. Because the patterns are generated electronically rather than mechanically embossed, the device can display an essentially unlimited range of text content, updating the tactile output in real time as the user reads.

### Wearing Mechanism

On the rear of the main body, a ring-shaped wearing member is provided, designed to be worn around the index finger. This wearing configuration was specifically chosen to optimize usability: with the device secured to the index finger, the user's thumb remains free to glide across the front-mounted touch and haptic panels. This thumb-based reading motion closely mimics the natural motion used in traditional braille reading, allowing users to intuitively adopt the device without extensive retraining. The ring-shaped design also ensures the device remains securely and comfortably positioned during extended use, leaving the user's other fingers and hand largely unencumbered for other tasks.

### NFC-Based Location Guidance

In addition to its text-reading capabilities, the device incorporates a Near Field Communication (NFC) module, enabling it to receive location-based guide information from NFC tags installed in the surrounding environment. Such tags may be strategically placed at locations of interest to blind users, including:

- **Roads and sidewalks**, providing directional or safety information
- **Intersections**, indicating crossing signals, street names, or traffic conditions
- **Stores and commercial establishments**, offering information about the business, entrance location, or available services
- **Existing braille signage**, allowing the device to supplement or digitally reproduce information already present in physical braille form

When the device is brought into proximity with an NFC tag, it automatically retrieves the associated data and renders it as a haptic pattern on the electro-sensitive panel, allowing the user to read the guide information immediately through touch, without needing to locate and physically interpret a separate braille sign.

## Advantages and Effects

This integrated design offers several significant benefits for blind and visually impaired users:

1. **Portability and Convenience**: The compact, wearable form factor allows users to carry and use the device throughout their daily routine, enabling them to read news articles, digital books, text messages, and other written content anytime and anywhere, without dependency on bulky braille materials or fixed installations.

2. **Intuitive Operation**: By positioning the wearing member on the index finger and the reading surface beneath the thumb, the device leverages natural hand movements familiar to braille readers, minimizing the learning curve associated with adopting new assistive technology.

3. **Enhanced Navigation and Situational Awareness**: The NFC-based guide information feature allows users to receive real-time, location-specific information as they move through public spaces, improving their ability to navigate independently and safely.

4. **Reduced Reliance on Physical Braille Infrastructure**: Because the device can digitally reproduce the content of existing braille signs via NFC tags, it extends the reach and accessibility of location-based information even in areas where physical braille signage may be absent, damaged, or difficult to locate.

5. **Improved Independence and Quality of Life**: By combining on-demand text reading with contextual location guidance in a single, easy-to-use wearable device, this disclosure significantly enhances the ability of blind and visually impaired individuals to access information and navigate their environment independently, contributing to greater autonomy and improved quality of life in daily activities.

Overall, this wearable haptic pattern display device represents a meaningful advancement in assistive technology, offering blind users a versatile, portable, and intuitive tool for both personal reading and environmental navigation.

# Understanding NFC Technology

Near Field Communication (NFC) is a short-range wireless technology that allows two devices to communicate when placed close together, typically within a few centimeters. The technology has become increasingly common in everyday life, powering contactless payments, transit cards, and quick data-sharing features between smartphones.

## How NFC Works

The underlying principle of NFC relies on electromagnetic induction between two loop antennas. When one device generates a small electrical current, it creates a magnetic field that the other device can detect. The receiving device then converts this signal into usable data. Because the range is so limited, NFC requires devices to be brought very close together, often just a tap away, which enhances both convenience and security.

## Common Applications

The most widespread use of NFC today is in mobile payment systems. Services like Apple Pay, Google Pay, and Samsung Pay all use NFC to let users pay for goods by simply tapping their phone near a payment terminal. Beyond payments, NFC is used in:

- **Public transportation** – Many transit systems use NFC-enabled cards or smartphones for fare payment.
- **Access control** – Office buildings and hotels increasingly use NFC-based key cards for secure entry.
- **Smart tags** – NFC tags embedded in posters, products, or business cards can trigger actions like opening a website or displaying information when scanned.
- **Device pairing** – Some Bluetooth speakers and headphones use NFC to simplify the pairing process with smartphones.

## Security Considerations

The short range of NFC communication provides a natural layer of security since would-be attackers would need to be in extremely close physical proximity to intercept a signal. Nevertheless, developers have added additional layers such as tokenization and encryption in payment systems to further reduce risks associated with data interception or fraud.

## The Future of NFC

The, as a technology that continues to evolve, NFC is expected to expand its role beyond payments and identification. Emerging applications include smart packaging that lets consumers verify product authenticity, healthcare devices for tracking medication adherence, and even connected home systems where NFC tags trigger custom automation routines. As more devices incorporate NFC chips, the technology is likely to become an even more integral part of daily digital interactions.

# Patent Disclosure Summary

## Title
**Wearable Haptic Device and Method for Tactile Text Rendering to Facilitate Reading by Visually Impaired Users**

---

## Field of the Invention
This disclosure relates to assistive technology devices, specifically to a wearable haptic apparatus that converts digital or optically-captured text into dynamic tactile textures, enabling blind and visually impaired users to "read" text through touch in real time.

---

## Background

Current solutions for text access by blind individuals include:
- **Braille displays**: Effective but expensive, bulky, limited to trained Braille readers, and typically stationary
- **Text-to-speech (audio) systems**: Widely used but lack privacy, compete with ambient sound awareness, and do not convey formatting, spatial layout, or non-linguistic cues
- **Braille literacy limitations**: Only a minority of blind individuals are fluent in Braille

There exists an unmet need for a compact, wearable device that renders text as intuitive tactile patterns without requiring Braille literacy, while preserving privacy and situational audio awareness.

---

## Summary of the Invention

The disclosed invention is a **wearable haptic reading device**, worn on the fingertip, palm, or wrist, that:

1. **Captures text** via an integrated camera, external scanning module, or wireless data input (e.g., from a smartphone app or e-reader)
2. **Processes the text** using onboard OCR (optical character recognition) and a text-to-texture mapping algorithm
3. **Renders tactile output** through a high-resolution array of microactuators (piezoelectric, electromagnetic, or pneumatic) that generate varying:
   - Vibration frequencies
   - Pressure intensities
   - Spatial patterns
   - Temporal sequences (temporal "stroke" patterns mimicking letterforms)
4. **Adapts in real time** to reading speed, letter spacing, and word boundaries based on user finger movement across a physical page or virtual scroll gesture

Unlike traditional Braille, which requires learning a discrete symbolic code, the device can optionally render **shape-based tactile representations** of letterforms (tracing the actual contour of characters) or **customizable abstract texture-to-phoneme mappings**, allowing for a gentler learning curve.

---

## Key Technical Components

| Component | Function |
|---|---|
| **Microactuator Array** | Grid of 16–64+ actuators delivering spatially distinct tactile stimuli |
| **OCR/Text Processing Unit** | Embedded or paired-device processor converting text to actuator instructions |
| **Motion/Position Sensor** | Tracks finger movement over source material or virtual interface for adaptive pacing |
| **Haptic Rendering Engine** | Software module mapping characters to texture, vibration, and shape patterns |
| **Wireless Communication Module** | Bluetooth/Wi-Fi for pairing with smartphones, e-readers, or smart glasses |
| **Power & Housing** | Rechargeable battery, ergonomic wearable form factor (ring, glove, wristband) |

---

## Novel Aspects (Claims Focus)

1. **Dynamic letterform tracing**: A method wherein actuators sequentially activate to trace the physical stroke path of a letter, rather than relying solely on static Braille dot patterns.
2. **Adaptive reading speed calibration**: A system that adjusts tactile output timing based on real-time finger velocity across text.
3. **Multi-modal texture encoding**: Combining vibration frequency, amplitude, and spatial actuator patterning to encode phonemes, whole words, or punctuation—reducing cognitive load versus single-modality Braille.
4. **Modular actuator array**: A reconfigurable/replaceable microactuator grid enabling different resolutions (e.g., fingertip-only vs. palm-wide arrays) for different literacy levels or reading speeds.
5. **Hybrid input integration**: Seamless switching between physical page scanning (camera-based) and digital text streaming (Bluetooth from e-reader/screen reader software).

---

## Potential Embodiments

- **Fingertip thimble/ring** with built-in micro-camera for scanning printed text line-by-line
- **Glove-based array** covering multiple fingers for parallel word-chunk reading
- **Wristband unit** paired with smart glasses for hands-free document scanning and haptic relay
- **Tablet/case attachment** for direct digital text reading without physical print materials

---

## Advantages Over Prior Art

- No Braille literacy required (optional letterform tracing mode)
- Preserves auditory awareness (unlike audio-based reading aids)
- Enables private, silent reading in public settings
- Compact and low-power compared to full Braille display panels
- Adaptable to multiple languages and symbol sets via software update (no hardware change needed)

---

## Industrial Applicability

Applicable to consumer assistive technology, educational tools for blind students, workplace accessibility equipment, and integration with existing screen-reader ecosystems (JAWS, VoiceOver, NVDA) as a tactile-output alternative or supplement.

---

*This summary is intended for internal review and preliminary patentability assessment. Formal claims, drawings, and prior art search to be completed prior to filing.*

# BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION

## Field of the Invention

The present disclosure relates generally to tactile information display devices, and more particularly to a finger-worn haptic display apparatus incorporating dynamically actuated tactile elements arranged to simulate Braille-like character patterns, in combination with near field communication (NFC) circuitry for wireless data acquisition and content delivery.

## Description of the Related Art

Braille remains a primary means by which visually impaired individuals access written text, signage, and other printed information. Conventional Braille displays typically employ a static array of raised dots formed on a fixed surface, such as embossed paper, printed Braille labels, or dedicated refreshable Braille display devices. These conventional approaches present several limitations that the present invention seeks to address.

Refreshable Braille displays, which utilize electromechanical or piezoelectric actuators to raise and lower pins in a Braille cell configuration, are widely used for reading digital text. However, existing refreshable Braille devices are generally implemented as standalone desktop units or as attachments to computing devices, resulting in bulky form factors that are not readily portable and cannot be worn on the body during normal activities. Such devices often require external tethering to a computer or mobile device via wired connections, further limiting their utility in mobile or ambulatory contexts. Additionally, many existing devices are configured to display only pre-loaded or manually input text, lacking a convenient mechanism for acquiring content from real-world objects, product packaging, informational placards, or other tagged sources encountered in daily life.

Efforts to miniaturize tactile displays for wearable applications have encountered numerous technical challenges, including the difficulty of packaging multiple independently actuated tactile elements within a housing small enough to be worn on a finger while maintaining sufficient spacing and displacement of tactile elements to be perceptible and distinguishable by touch. Power consumption and battery life present further constraints, as actuators capable of producing perceptible tactile deflections often require more current than can be practically supplied by a battery of a size suitable for a finger-worn device.

Separately, near field communication technology has become widely deployed for short-range wireless data exchange, enabling devices to read information from passive NFC tags embedded in products, signage, transit cards, and similar objects. Despite the proliferation of NFC-tagged content in public and commercial environments, this content is predominantly presented in visual form, such as text displayed on a paired smartphone screen, and is not natively accessible to visually impaired users without additional screen-reading software or audio output, which may be undesirable in noisy environments or situations requiring auditory attention for safety or privacy reasons.

Accordingly, there remains an unmet need for a compact, wearable tactile display device capable of being worn directly on a finger, that can wirelessly acquire textual or symbolic information from nearby NFC-enabled sources, and that can convert such information into a Braille-like tactile pattern perceptible to the wearer in real time, without reliance on auditory output, external tethering, or bulky standalone hardware. The present invention addresses these and other deficiencies of the prior art.

# Patent Abstract

**COMPACT WEARABLE HAPTIC TEXT CONVERSION DEVICE FOR VISUALLY IMPAIRED USERS**

A compact wearable device for converting textual information into discernible haptic patterns is disclosed, enabling visually impaired users to perceive written content through tactile feedback. The device comprises a housing configured for wearable attachment to a user's body, an integrated touch screen interface configured to receive user input and facilitate navigation through device functions via tactile and gesture-based controls, and a near-field communication (NFC) tag reader configured to detect and retrieve textual data encoded within proximate NFC tags. The device further includes a processing unit operatively coupled to the touch screen and NFC reader, the processing unit configured to receive text data from at least one of the touch screen interface, the NFC tag reader, or an external data source, and to convert the received text data into a corresponding sequence of haptic output signals according to a predetermined encoding scheme. A haptic actuator array, disposed within or upon the housing in contact with the user's skin, is configured to generate distinguishable vibrational, pressure-based, or thermal patterns corresponding to individual characters, words, or phrases represented in the text data, thereby enabling the user to interpret textual information through tactile sensation alone. The device may further include a power source, wireless communication module for connectivity with external devices, and a memory unit for storing encoding schemes, user preferences, and cached textual data. The compact form factor permits unobtrusive wearing, and the combined touch screen and NFC functionality allows for versatile text acquisition from both direct user input and tagged physical objects, providing an accessible, portable, and independent means for visually impaired individuals to access written information in daily environments.

---

*Note: This abstract is provided as a drafting template/example for illustrative purposes. For an actual patent filing, this document should be reviewed and refined by a registered patent attorney or agent to ensure compliance with USPTO or relevant jurisdictional formatting requirements, proper claim support, and accurate technical specificity based on the actual invention details.*

# PATENT APPLICATION

## TITLE OF INVENTION
**Ring-Mounted Tactile Reading Device with Near-Field Communication for Text Perception and Location Guidance for Visually Impaired Users**

---

## FIELD OF THE INVENTION

The present invention relates generally to assistive technology devices for persons with visual impairments, and more particularly to a wearable ring-form-factor apparatus mounted on the index finger that converts printed or displayed text into tactile or electro-tactile sensory output, and further incorporates near-field communication (NFC) capabilities for reading environmental location guide tags to assist with spatial navigation and orientation.

---

## BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION

Persons who are blind or visually impaired have historically relied upon Braille embossed materials, audio description systems, or human-assisted reading to access printed text. Braille literacy rates have declined in many populations due to limited availability of Braille-embossed materials, cost of transcription, and the physical bulk of Braille documents. Audio-based reading solutions, including screen readers and optical character recognition (OCR) devices coupled with text-to-speech synthesis, provide an alternative but suffer from disadvantages including auditory fatigue, inability to function in noisy environments, lack of privacy in public or shared reading contexts, and interference with the user's ability to simultaneously perceive ambient auditory cues necessary for safe navigation.

Furthermore, existing navigation aids for visually impaired individuals, such as white canes, guide dogs, and GPS-based applications, provide limited granularity with respect to indoor wayfinding and identification of specific locations, rooms, or objects marked with discrete signage.

There exists an unmet need for a compact, unobtrusive, hands-capable device that enables direct tactile perception of text content without occupying the auditory channel, while simultaneously providing a means for identifying and interpreting location-specific guide markers embedded within a built environment.

---

## SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION

The present invention provides a ring-mounted wearable apparatus configured to be worn on the index finger (or other digit) of a user, comprising a tactile or electro-tactile output surface positioned on an underside or fingertip-facing portion of the device, an optical or image-capture sensor for detecting printed or displayed text, a processing unit configured to convert detected text into a tactile character encoding scheme or a real-time electro-tactile stimulation pattern corresponding to letterforms or Braille-equivalent symbols, and a near-field communication (NFC) module configured to detect and read passive or active NFC tags affixed to environmental structures, signage, or objects, thereby providing the user with location-identifying information.

In one embodiment, the tactile output is generated through an array of micro-actuators (e.g., piezoelectric, electromagnetic, or shape-memory alloy actuators) arranged beneath a contact surface positioned against the pad of the index finger, said actuators being selectively energized to reproduce raised patterns simulating Braille cells or alphanumeric shapes as the finger is swept across text.

In another embodiment, the tactile output is generated through localized electro-tactile stimulation, wherein an array of electrodes delivers controlled, sub-perceptual-injury electrical impulses to the skin of the fingertip, said impulses being modulated in amplitude, frequency, and spatial location to create a perceptible sensation corresponding to character shapes or Braille-dot configurations.

The device further comprises a rechargeable power source, a wireless communication module for optional connection to external computing devices, and a control interface allowing the user to adjust reading speed, sensitivity, and output modality.

---

## BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF THE DRAWINGS

*(In an actual filing, drawings would accompany the following descriptions.)*

- **FIG. 1** depicts a perspective view of the ring-mounted device as worn on a user's index finger.
- **FIG. 2** depicts an exploded view of the device housing, showing the sensor module, tactile/electro-tactile actuator array, processing unit, NFC antenna, and power source.
- **FIG. 3** is a block diagram illustrating the functional architecture of the device, including signal flow from the optical sensor through the processing unit to the tactile output array.
- **FIG. 4** illustrates the NFC tag reading process as the device is brought into proximity with an environmental guide tag.
- **FIG. 5** depicts an alternative embodiment employing electro-tactile electrode arrays in place of mechanical actuators.

---

## DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF THE INVENTION

### 1. General Configuration

Referring to FIG. 1, the device (100) comprises a ring-shaped housing (101) sized and shaped to be worn on the index finger (102) of a user, in a manner analogous to a conventional finger ring, but incorporating a functional module (103) positioned over or adjacent to the fingertip or finger pad region. The housing (101) may be manufactured from a lightweight, durable, and skin-safe material, including but not limited to medical-grade silicone, polycarbonate, or anodized aluminum, and may be provided in multiple sizes or with an adjustable band to accommodate varying finger diameters.

### 2. Text Detection Subsystem

The device incorporates an optical sensing subsystem (110), which may comprise a miniature camera module, photodiode array, or line-scan optical sensor, positioned on the housing such that it is oriented toward a reading surface when the user's finger is placed upon or swept across printed text, a display screen, or other text-bearing medium. The optical sensing subsystem (110) is operatively coupled to a processing unit (120) comprising a microcontroller or application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC), which executes optical character recognition (OCR) algorithms to identify alphanumeric characters, symbols, or Braille-equivalent representations present within the captured optical data.

In an alternative embodiment, the device may be configured to detect text through direct electrical or capacitive coupling with a touch-sensitive display screen, wherein the device receives text data directly from the display device via a wireless or NFC-based data exchange, obviating the need for optical character recognition.

### 3. Tactile Output Subsystem

The processing unit (120) is configured to convert recognized text characters into a control signal sequence corresponding to a tactile encoding scheme. In one embodiment, said encoding scheme comprises a Braille-cell representation, wherein each recognized character is mapped to a corresponding six-dot or eight-dot Braille pattern. In another embodiment, the encoding scheme comprises a direct tactile representation of the letterform itself, wherein the shape of the alphanumeric character is reproduced through sequential or simultaneous actuation of the tactile array.

The tactile output subsystem (130) comprises an array of micro-actuators arranged in a grid pattern beneath a finger-contacting surface (131). Each micro-actuator is independently addressable and configured to produce a localized raised or depressed deformation of the contacting surface (131), said deformation being perceptible to the mechanoreceptors of the user's fingertip. The micro-actuators may comprise piezoelectric bending elements, electromagnetic solenoid pins, shape-memory alloy wires, or micro-electromechanical system (MEMS)-based actuators.

### 4. Electro-Tactile Alternative Embodiment

Referring to FIG. 5, in an alternative embodiment, the tactile output subsystem (130) is replaced with an electro-tactile stimulation array (530) comprising a plurality of independently addressable electrodes (531) positioned in contact with the skin of the user's fingertip. The processing unit (120) is configured to deliver controlled electrical stimulation pulses to selected electrodes (531), said pulses being characterized by amplitude, pulse-width, and frequency parameters selected to produce a perceptible, non-damaging tactile sensation. The spatial pattern of electrode activation corresponds to the recognized character or Braille-cell configuration, such that sequential activation across the array, synchronized with the natural sweeping motion of the finger across text, produces a perceived tactile representation of the text content.

### 5. Near-Field Communication Subsystem

The device further comprises a near-field communication (NFC) module (140) integrated within the housing (101), said NFC module comprising an antenna coil and NFC transceiver chip configured to detect, read, and optionally write data to passive or active NFC tags (150) positioned within the environment. Said NFC tags (150) may be affixed to doorways, room placards, elevator panels, transit signage, product packaging, or other location-relevant or object-relevant structures, and may encode information including, without limitation, room identification, directional guidance, hazard warnings, or descriptive metadata.

Upon bringing the device (100) into proximity with an NFC tag (150), typically within a range of approximately 0 to 10 centimeters, the NFC module (140) establishes a communication link and retrieves the encoded data payload. The processing unit (120) is configured to convert the retrieved data into a tactile or electro-tactile output via the tactile output subsystem (130), analogous to the text-reading function described above, thereby enabling the user to perceive location-identifying or navigational information through the same tactile interface used for general text reading.

### 6. Auxiliary Components

The device further comprises:

- A wireless communication module (170), such as a Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) transceiver, configured to enable pairing with an external computing device (e.g., a smartphone) for firmware updates, configuration adjustments, or supplemental audio output;

- An inertial measurement unit (IMU) (190), configured to detect finger motion and orientation, thereby enabling the processing unit (120) to synchronize tactile output timing with the natural sweeping or scanning motion of the user's finger across a text surface.

### 7. Method of Operation

In operation, a user wearing the device (100) on the index finger (102) places the finger upon a printed page, display screen, or NFC-tagged object. The optical sensing subsystem (110) or NFC module (140), as applicable, detects the presence of text or tag data. The processing unit (120) processes the detected information and generates a corresponding tactile or electro-tactile output pattern via the tactile output subsystem (130), which is perceived by the user's fingertip. The user may sweep the finger across a line of text in a manner analogous to reading Braille, receiving sequential tactile representations of each character or word, or may hold the device in proximity to an NFC tag to receive location-identifying tactile output.

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose the "Field of the Invention" and "Summary" portions of a patent for an assistive technology device that displays braille-like haptic textures and reads NFC tags for navigation assistance.
counterfactuals.output:
# FIELD OF THE INVENTION

The present invention relates generally to assistive technology devices for individuals with visual impairments, and more particularly to a portable haptic feedback device that combines tactile braille-like texture rendering with near-field communication (NFC) tag reading capabilities to provide real-time navigation assistance, location identification, and contextual information delivery to users in indoor and outdoor environments.

---

# SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION

The present invention provides an assistive technology device designed to enhance the independence and mobility of visually impaired individuals by combining tactile braille-like haptic output with NFC-based environmental sensing and navigation assistance.

In one embodiment, the device comprises a housing containing a haptic display surface constructed from an array of dynamically actuated pins, pads, or piezoelectric elements capable of forming raised, braille-like tactile patterns. This tactile surface is configured to render alphanumeric characters, directional indicators, symbolic icons, and other perceptible textures that convey information to the user through touch, without requiring auditory output, though auditory output may optionally be provided as a supplementary or alternative feedback modality.

The device further includes an NFC reader module configured to detect and read data from NFC tags positioned at fixed locations throughout an environment, such as building entrances, hallway intersections, elevators, transit stations, or points of interest. Upon detection of an NFC tag, the device retrieves associated location data, navigational instructions, or descriptive metadata encoded on or linked to the tag, which is then processed by an onboard controller and translated into corresponding haptic output patterns on the tactile display.

In accordance with certain embodiments, the device includes a processor operatively coupled to the NFC reader and the haptic display, the processor being configured to: (a) receive signal data from a scanned NFC tag; (b) decode the signal data into a set of navigational or informational content; (c) convert the decoded content into a haptic rendering sequence compatible with the braille-like tactile display; and (d) actuate the tactile display to present the rendered content to the user in real time.

Additional embodiments may incorporate wireless communication modules for interfacing with a remote server, mobile application, or cloud-based database, enabling dynamic updating of navigational content, crowd-sourced tag location data, or personalized route information. The device may further include an inertial measurement unit, vibration motor, or auxiliary feedback mechanism for supplementing directional guidance, as well as a rechargeable power source, ergonomic handheld or wearable housing, and user-configurable settings for adjusting haptic sensitivity, refresh rate, or output language.

In some embodiments, the device is configured to operate in conjunction with a network of distributed NFC tags forming a navigation infrastructure within a building or public space, such that the user may progressively scan tags along a route to receive turn-by-turn tactile guidance, points-of-interest identification, hazard warnings, or emergency information.

The present invention thereby provides a novel and useful combination of tactile braille-rendering technology and NFC-based positional sensing, offering an assistive navigation solution that is non-visual, non-auditory-dependent, portable, and adaptable to a wide range of indoor and outdoor navigation scenarios, thereby improving accessibility and independent mobility for visually impaired users.
